item.title: Deep Principle Releases Hydrogen-1.0: A 753B Open-Weight Model for Scientific Discovery
item.abstract: Deep Principle has released Hydrogen-1.0 , an open-weight scientific model for chemistry, materials science and life sciences. It is built by post-training Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 on domain data, laboratory records and agent discovery trajectories. For developers, it offers open weights that report a FrontierScience-Research win over GPT-6-Astra. The weights ship under the MIT License. Hydrogen-1.0 is a scientific research assistant model from Deep Principle, a Hangzhou-based AI-for-materials company. The model card describes it as a GLM-5.3 derivative for scientific problem solving. It targets question framing, experiment planning, results analysis and open-ended discovery. Deep Principle team states that proprietary models produced recent AI science results, but their discovery capabilities are not open. Hydrogen-1.0 is its attempt at a reproducible, inspectable alternative. The pipeline combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL). Data comes from 4 sources: Infrastructure builds on Megatron and SGLang across NVIDIA CUDA and AMD ROCm. The team keeps dynamic sparse attention causal across context-parallel shards. Muon optimizer state is moved between CPU, GPU and disk per backend. RL uses resumable rollouts, and each token keeps its original behavior log-probability for importance correction. A layout adapter converts training checkpoints into BF16 and 128×128 blockwise FP8 inference weights. Full datasets and recipes are not released. On public benchmarks, Deep Principle reports Hydrogen-1.0 outperforms GPT-6-Astra on FrontierScience-Research. The tweet thread from one of the founders’ report 93.0% on GPQA-Diamond. That improves on GLM-5.3 and roughly matches Kimi-K3, per the blog. Internal research-task evals compare it with GPT-6-Astra at maximum thinking: In transition metal complex design, models chased a larger HOMO-LUMO gap over 5 rounds. By round 5, Hydrogen-1.0 reached a mean best-so-far gap of 4.318 eV. GPT-6-Astra reached 3.689 eV and Kimi-K3 reached 3.353 eV. On 117 experiment-planning questions, Hydrogen-1.0 scored above Kimi-K3. GPT-6-Astra and Opus-5.5 were excluded after refusing more than 50% of requests. The technical post shows 4 demos . Hydrogen-1.0 writes Python to build a polyethylene melt and runs GROMACS. It detects a topology error, repairs it, and analyzes the corrected 40 ns trajectory. It grows an Ireland-Claisen reaction network of 27 structures through 30 plausible reactions. It ranks 7 candidate monoformylation products of 2-bromonaphthalene from a 1H NMR trace. It also writes a JSON protocol for a 12-vial Suzuki coupling study. A virtual lab compilation step catches an aspiration without a fresh tip before execution. Weights are on Hugging Face and ModelScope . Deep Principle team tested BF16 serving with SGLang on 8 GPUs using tensor parallelism of 8. NVFP4 targets NVIDIA B200 and B300. MXFP4 targets AMD Instinct MI350X and MI355X. The server exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with a reasoning_effort setting. item.title: Build efficient agents with knowledge distillation on Amazon SageMaker AI
item.abstract: You built a shopping assistant on a frontier model, and it works. A shopper asks for “a black waist bag under twenty dollars from a shop with at least 4.5 stars,” and the agent searches the catalog, inspects candidates, checks the constraints, and commits to a recommendation. But what does that interaction actually cost? An agentic assistant is not one model call, it is a loop: search, read results, refine, verify, decide. A single completed task can be multiple calls to that frontier model, and you pay for every one, on every shopper. At production scale, that per-task cost compounds, erodes the project’s ROI, and stops the project from shipping. One way to make an agentic application more efficient is to use a smaller model, which is faster to respond and more cost-effective to host. The catch is quality: a smaller model usually falls short on the task, which is why the larger one was chosen in the first place. Knowledge distillation closes that gap by transferring the behavior of the larger “teacher” model into a smaller “student”, training the student to reproduce the teacher’s outputs, so it keeps much of the quality at the smaller model’s speed and cost. In this post you will learn how to use knowledge distillation, and specifically sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD), to fine-tune a shopping agent on Amazon SageMaker AI . We cover how to generate high-quality multi-step trajectories with a frontier teacher and keep the ones that solve the task, how to encode them for supervised fine-tuning, how to run the training on serverless infrastructure, and how to evaluate the student against a held-out benchmark. Figure 1: One agentic task is a loop, not a single call: the agent searches, reads results, refines, verifies, and decides, and each step is a separate billed call to the frontier model. A single completed task can be multiple calls, on every shopper The simplest applicable form of distillation is sequence-level knowledge distillation (SeqKD). It uses a teacher model to generate high-quality responses, then trains a student model on those responses with supervised fine-tuning (SFT). SeqKD needs only the teacher’s text , with no access to teacher logits and no reinforcement-learning infrastructure, so it works even with a closed or API-only teacher. Compared to other approaches such as logit-based or on-policy, it sits at the most cost-effective and portable end of the distillation spectrum. The teacher writes the answers, and the student is fine-tuned on them. Because those answers persist as a dataset, you can reuse them to train or test different students without regenerating the data. In principle, you would want the student to match the teacher’s full distribution over possible outputs. The caveat here is that you can’t. The space of possible sequences is astronomically large, so matching it exactly isn’t feasible. SeqKD sidesteps that by approximating it with samples the teacher actually produces. For an agent, the sequence the teacher produces is not a block of prose but a trajectory, an ordered run of reasoning, tool calls, and the observations they return, where each step is conditioned on everything before it. Training the student on that whole sequence teaches it the reasoning that leads to each action and the multi-step course of action itself, not a single paragraph of answer text. That makes an agentic task one of the cleanest illustrations of sequence-level KD, because the sequence being copied is the behavior itself. Figure 2: SeqKD transfers behavior through the teacher’s text outputs alone: the teacher generates trajectories, the student trains on them, and the result keeps much of the teacher’s quality at the small model’s speed and cost. No teacher weights, logits, or gradients are required during training, so it runs as ordinary supervised fine-tuning SeqKD fits a specific set of situations: You have the inputs but no high-quality target outputs This is the core case for SeqKD, which is fundamentally data generation. You supply the inputs, and the teacher writes the targets, so you can fine-tune on a task or domain that has no existing high-quality labels. The targets can be as simple as single answers or as involved as multi-turn tool-use trajectories. This post takes the demanding end of that spectrum, agentic trajectories, which are especially hard to source. A single task branches into many partially correct runs, and telling a solved run from a failed one takes a reliable grader. A benchmark with a programmatic scorer supplies exactly that, so you can let the teacher generate trajectories and keep only the ones that solve the task. Your teacher is a frontier model you can only reach through an API This is the normal case for frontier models. You can’t access the weights to host it yourself, you can’t read its logits, and you can’t fine-tune it. That rules out logit-based distillation and on-policy methods, which all need that internal access. SeqKD needs only the teacher’s text responses, so it is the one approach that still works, and it frees you from paying frontier prices on every request after the student takes over. You want a strong, cost-effective first step Some of the strongest small reasoning models were built in significant part with SeqKD (supervised fine-tuning on teacher reasoning traces), so it is an effective starting point for reasoning transfer when the setup is right. The DeepSeek-R1 distilled models are a well-known example: the reasoning of a large teacher was distilled into smaller Qwen and Llama students by fine-tuning them on the teacher’s generated reasoning traces. To run this example, you need: This section walks the pipeline from end to end. A frontier teacher, GLM-5.3 on Amazon Bedrock, acts as the ShoppingBench agent to generate trajectories. The benchmark’s own scorer keeps only the ones that solve the task, and those solved trajectories fine-tune a Qwen3.5-4B student with serverless supervised fine-tuning on SageMaker AI model customization. The distilled student is then evaluated on a held-out ShoppingBench split and served behind a SageMaker AI Inference real-time endpoint that runs the tool loop. Figure 3: Distilling a shopping agent on Amazon SageMaker AI: a frontier teacher on Amazon Bedrock acts as the ShoppingBench agent on the training problems, ShoppingBench’s own scorer keeps only the trajectories that solve the task (rejection sampling), each solved trajectory is encoded per step, the student is fine-tuned serverlessly with Amazon SageMaker AI model customization, and the result is evaluated on the held-out ShoppingBench test split Sourcing trajectories worth imitating is the hard part, and the ShoppingBench scorer is what separates the successful runs from the failed ones. ShoppingBench publishes 750 synthesized shopping problems, 250 each for the product, shop, and voucher intents, each with a hidden gold answer and the constraints that define success. We split them once into 426 training problems and 324 held-out evaluation problems (product 103, shop 105, voucher 116), as fixed indices so the two sets don’t overlap. For each training problem, a frontier teacher, GLM-5.3 on Amazon Bedrock with reasoning on and temperature 1.0, acts as the ShoppingBench agent. It searches the catalog of about 2.7 million products, inspects candidates, and recommends the ones that meet the constraints. We sample the teacher twice per problem, which gives 850 trajectories, then let ShoppingBench’s own scorer keep only the ones that solve the task. Temperature 1.0 is deliberate. Sampling rather than greedy decoding makes the two attempts explore different queries and reasoning paths, which gives more problems at least one solved trajectory and a more diverse set to learn from. This rejection-sampling step turns a capable-but-imperfect teacher into a clean training set, since the teacher only has to be right often enough that the solved runs are worth imitating.

item.title: NVIDIA Releases Auto Ontology: An Open Semantic Layer That Grounds AI Agent SQL
item.abstract: NVIDIA has released Auto Ontology , an open library under the Apache 2.0 license . NVIDIA Auto Ontology is a semantic layer framework that builds a context layer from enterprise metadata. Agents use that layer to write SQL against certified business definitions. The repository states the problem plainly: a fast revenue answer is worthless if the number is wrong. It is a context layer that sits between an agent and the data warehouse. It tells the agent where data lives and what fields mean. It also says whether to use a field, how to use it, and where it came from. NVIDIA’s developer page frames the output as a starting ontology. Business experts still test, refine and certify it. The stack has 4 core services. A Next.js 16 frontend handles the web UI and authentication on port 3000. A FastAPI backend with LangChain runs chat, NL-to-SQL and catalog APIs on port 3001. An ingestion worker writes embeddings on port 3002. Postgres with pgvector stores the catalog, the ontology and the vectors. Source databases can be Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake or DuckDB. Models are set through environment “triplets” of endpoint, key and model. Separate roles exist for reasoning, non-reasoning, embedding and reranking. Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works. The MCP server docs describe 9 read-only tools. ask_question returns the answer, the SQL and the rows as separate fields. Results cap at 100 rows. check_readiness confirms a compiled semantic layer and a live database connection exist. There is no tool for browsing raw schemas. NVIDIA chose that on purpose, so agents reach data through the semantic layer. The underlying OpenAPI spec publishes 87 operations. Sign-in runs through OAuth, and every call carries the signed-in user’s permissions. NVIDIA ships a separate harness, auto-ontology-eval . It runs 2 arms in NeMo Gym: a schema-only LLM control and the ontology-grounded agent. Scoring is deterministic execution match, with no LLM judge. Bundled datasets include BIRD Dev (1,534 questions, 11 databases) and Mini-Dev (500 questions). FDABench-Lite adds 169 questions, and BEAVER defaults to a 100-question sample. The harness repo adds 2 limitations. Optional few-shot exemplars and value anchors go to the ontology arm only. A delta measured with them covers those inputs, not grounding alone. Its tested configuration also routes both arms through a Claude model on NVIDIA’s inference gateway. Local setup is docker compose up -d --build after filling in .env . Kubernetes users get a Helm chart and a DEPLOYMENT.md guide. NVIDIA team also publishes the backend as an NGC container . An NVIDIA API key from build.nvidia.com covers the default models. Check out the GitHub repo , the eval harness and the MCP docs . Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . item.title: Running LLMs Locally Does Not Mean Your Data Is Safe: What Cohere’s Study Reveals
item.abstract: Running LLMs Locally Does Not Mean Your Data Is Safe: What Cohere’s Study Reveals Cohere caught Alibaba’s Qwen model unexpectedly attempting to upload a test payload to Alibaba Cloud storage during a cybersecurity task, but the sandbox blocked the request, leaving questions about what triggered the behavior. By Abid Ali Awan , KDnuggets Assistant Editor on November 2, 2026 in Language Models Running a large language model (LLM) locally is often considered the safest option for developers who want more control over their data. You download the model weights, run everything on your own hardware, and avoid sending sensitive information to external AI providers. But does that automatically make your AI system secure? A recent investigation by Cohere has raised some interesting questions. During a security benchmark, researchers observed an open-weight Qwen model attempting to send data to an Alibaba Cloud server, despite receiving no instructions to do so. The findings quickly sparked a debate about model security, training data, and whether running LLMs locally really protects users. I think there is more to this story than blaming a single model. Let us look at what actually happened, what the community thinks, and why the entire AI agent setup matters. What Did Cohere Find? On October 26, 2026, Cohere published an investigation into unusual behavior from Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next , an open-weight language model. The researchers were evaluating the model using Microsoft's CTI-REALM cybersecurity benchmark. The assigned task was straightforward: write a detection rule to identify suspicious commands that download and execute malicious shell scripts. Instead, the model unexpectedly started exploring its environment. According to Cohere, it inspected temporary files, checked available command-line utilities, examined DNS configuration, and attempted to upload a test payload to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket located in Beijing. What made this particularly interesting was that the model's visible reasoning indicated that it would not execute any tools. Fortunately, the researchers were using an isolated sandbox without outbound network access, so the upload attempt failed. The payload was also a fixed test string, not demonstrated private user data. Cohere reported that this behavior occurred in fewer than one in 100,000 evaluation calls . Repeating the same original prompt produced a normal detection rule. The investigation therefore demonstrates a rare and unexpected tool action. It does not prove that Alibaba deliberately introduced a backdoor or that sensitive information was successfully leaked. What Does the AI Community Think? Cohere's investigation sparked heated discussions across Reddit's LocalLLaMA community and LinkedIn , with developers questioning both the findings and the reproduction methodology. One major criticism focused on prefilling . Cohere's released script supplies 2,323 tokens of previously recorded reasoning and commands, stopping just before URL generation. Critics argued that this setup effectively encourages the model to complete a suspicious command rather than demonstrating that it would independently initiate one. However, Cohere clarified on Reddit that the original incident occurred without prefilling. The technique was introduced afterward to investigate the behavior, which reportedly occurred in fewer than one in 100,000 evaluation calls. Other developers suggested that the Alibaba URLs might be training artifacts rather than evidence of malicious intent . Models exposed to agent logs, cloud storage commands, and similar examples during training could reproduce those patterns in unrelated tasks. Some community members also questioned whether proprietary models would exhibit similar behavior under identical tests. earlier community reports had already described unexpected Alibaba Cloud URLs appearing during normal Qwen usage, suggesting the phenomenon was not limited to Cohere's experiments. The debate also highlighted a broader concern: running an open-weight model locally does not automatically make an AI agent secure . Models with terminal access and unrestricted network permissions can still attempt unexpected operations, making sandboxing and network restrictions essential. Ultimately, the investigation raises legitimate questions about AI agent security, but the available evidence does not establish an intentional backdoor. Reproducing suspicious behavior and proving malicious intent are two very different things. Why Training Data Might Explain This Behavior One thing I find particularly interesting about this incident is how training data can influence an AI model's behavior, sometimes in unexpected ways. LLMs learn patterns from enormous amounts of text, code, conversations, and tool-use examples. If a model encounters thousands of examples involving particular cloud services, shell commands, or debugging workflows, it may reproduce similar patterns later. For example, a coding agent might associate debugging with downloading files or making network requests, even when those actions are unnecessary for the current task. This could explain why Qwen generated Alibaba Cloud URLs. The model may have learned those patterns from its training data rather than deliberately attempting to send information elsewhere. There is also the possibility of training-data poisoning , where malicious examples are introduced into training or fine-tuning data to influence future model behavior. However, these explanations remain speculative. We don't have enough evidence to determine what caused the behavior observed by Cohere. And that brings me to what I think is the more important issue: what happens when a model's unexpected output is allowed to execute? The Bigger Security Problem Is the Agent Harness A language model cannot independently access your files or send data over the internet. It needs tools and an execution environment that allow it to perform those actions. This is where the agent harness becomes important. The harness is the software surrounding the model. It manages context, tool execution, permissions, filesystem access, and interactions with external services. Think about coding agents such as Claude Code , Codex CLI , or other local agent systems. The model decides what action to propose, but the harness controls how that action is executed. If an agent has unrestricted terminal access, permission to read sensitive files, and outbound network access, an unexpected command can become a serious security problem. The same model running in an isolated environment might generate the identical command without being able to execute it successfully. There is research supporting this distinction. In the recent HarnessSecurity-Bench study, researchers evaluated security mechanisms across six coding-agent harnesses, including Claude Code, Codex CLI, and Qwen Code . Under their controlled testing conditions, enabling automatic tool approval increased attack success from 29.2% to 95.6% . That is a substantial difference caused by the security configuration of the agent system rather than a change to the underlying model. The researchers also found that network isolation and read-only execution reduced successful attacks, although these restrictions could make legitimate tasks harder to complete. This is why I think the discussion should go beyond whether Qwen intentionally generated a suspicious URL. How Can We Make Local AI Agents Safer? I don't think the solution is to stop using open-weight models. Instead, we need to be more careful about what our AI agents are allowed to do. Security experts at OWASP recommend sandboxing, restricting tool permissions, and limiting network access when deploying coding agents. Here are a few practical steps you can take: Run agents in a sandbox: Use Docker containers, virtual machines, or tools like Anthropic's Sandbox Runtime to isolate command execution.

item.title: Build World Models for Interactive Simulation with NVIDIA Cosmos
item.abstract:
Physical AI developers working with world models face two distinct challenges: adapting models to their sensors, tasks, and data, and getting those models into applications reliably. NVIDIA Cosmos addresses each. Cosmos is a platform of world foundation models and development tools for physical AI . Cosmos Framework provides agent skills and recipes for world model training, multimodal data processing, optimization and inference. Cosmos NIM microservices supports GPU-accelerated serving through application APIs. This post walks through both. The simulation section shows how to use Cosmos Framework’s inference recipes and agent skills to generate synchronized camera video and LiDAR observations for AV, robot, and surgical scenarios, starting from released checkpoints you can run today. The deployment section shows how to choose a NIM configuration for your GPU, launch the container, verify readiness, and send your first inference request. When to use Cosmos Framework for world model development Cosmos Framework is an open and fully modular framework for world model training, model optimization, and inference to support a full model development lifecycle using new agent skills. It is expanding beyond Cosmos 3 to support NVIDIA Alpamayo , GR00T, Qwen, pi0.5, and other compatible Hugging Face models. Training Train models on text, images, video, audio, and actions faster using new skills. Use LoRA for parameter-efficient adaptation, or full supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to update all model parameters. Load data through JSONL, WebDataset, LeRobot, or custom adapters and train across GPUs and save checkpoints to resume runs. Point your agent to post-training skill to accelerate and automate. Apply Reinforcement Learning The platform now covers online and offline RL paths . Newly supported pipelines include: DPO: offline preference optimization. GRPO: online RL with a rule or model reward and vLLM rollouts. PPO: actor-critic RL with frozen reference and critic, including RL for embodied policies in simulation. OPD: on-policy distillation from a frozen teacher. DiffusionNFT: online RL for diffusion world models. Run rollout, reward, and training roles on shared GPUs or separate pools. Connect supported simulators to collect experience. Optimize models and inference Distill models to reduce model size or generation steps; quantize models to reduce memory use. Run compatible checkpoints with Hugging Face Diffusers, PyTorch, SGLang, vLLM-Omni, vLLM, TRT-LLM and TRT-Edge-LLM or NVIDIA NIM. Evaluate for quality, accuracy and GPU usage and maximize compute utilization. Use agents with Cosmos Framework Load the setup, inference, post-training, and troubleshooting skills under .agents/skills . Give the agent a bounded task: Prompt : Post-train <checkpoint> on <dataset> using <recipe> . Pin all revisions, validate the dataset, and keep training and evaluation episodes separate. Run the smoke test, save the configuration, and stop at <N> GPU-hours. Export and compare against the base model on held-out data using three seeds. Repeat evaluation at a supported lower precision; record quality, peak memory, and latency. Which Cosmos simulation workflow should you use? Cosmos Framework provides post-training and inference recipes for robot simulation, realistic scene generation, multi-camera driving simulation, and surgical policy evaluation. New Cosmos 3 Nano simulation recipes and example checkpoints enable developers to use agent runnable skills to evaluate our example checkpoints and adapt Cosmos 3 Nano to custom sensors, action space, and data domains. These checkpoints support PyTorch and vLLM-Omni, tested on NVIDIA Hopper and Blackwell GPUs. Use the recipe to select GPU count, memory configuration, and inference settings. Autonomous vehicle simulation: Both AV checkpoints take a prompt and World Scenario Map (WSM) controls representing lanes, objects, road markings, traffic signs, and road boundaries. Joint RGB–LiDAR generation additionally uses HD-map rangemap controls and supports optional initial LiDAR observations. Prompts describe weather, lighting, time of day, road conditions with prefixes providing camera-rig and field-of-view context. An optional initial camera images provide visual context to guide the generated scene’s appearance. Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto uses bidirectional generation to denoise an entire multi-view clip at once for offline synthetic data generation . It supports 30 fps input and output video, with up to 400 frames at 480p or 720p; longer sequences can be generated through autoregressive chunking. Change the prompt to turn a daytime drive into a rainy night while keeping the same road layout and vehicle trajectories. Use these variations to train and evaluate perception and driving models across weather and lighting conditions. After Framework setup, run the four-GPU examples below from the repository root. item.title: Agentic engineering intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
item.abstract: When a qualified aerospace component goes obsolete or hits a long lead time, an engineer spends days cross-referencing specifications across vendor datasheets, interface control documents (ICDs), and qualification records before documenting a substitution justification for review. An incorrect substitution on a flight-critical component can cause mission failure, yet the evidence trail behind each decision is often spread across email and undocumented institutional knowledge, so there is no formal, repeatable package for a reviewer to check. A previous post, Manufacturing intelligence with Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings , showed how the model retrieves answers locked inside engineering diagrams, thermal plots, and datasheet charts that text-only pipelines miss. This post picks up where that retrieval work left off, putting those capabilities inside a multi-agent system that assembles substitution evidence, from retrieval to a drafted assessment. In this post, we show how to build a multi-agent engineering assistant that cuts the manual cross-referencing behind part substitution evaluation using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings , and the open source Strands Agents SDK . A planner routes work across three specialist agents that search a multimodal knowledge base, score candidates against deterministic tolerance rules, compare part photos, and ground lifecycle claims in live web data. The engineer remains the decision-maker throughout, because the system assembles evidence and drafts documents without ever approving a substitution on its own. The assistant is built around one design rule, which is that the engineer makes every decision and the system assembles the evidence for it. That rule determines where we use large language models (LLMs) and where we use deterministic code instead. Three pillars define the architecture: The following diagram shows the architecture. Figure 1: Architecture of the multi-agent engineering assistant on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. In this solution, chat requests from the engineer’s application flow into a multi-agent graph hosted on AgentCore runtime: a planner (Claude Haiku 5.5) produces a routing plan, specialists (Claude Sonnet 5.5) execute their tools, and a supervisor (Claude Opus 5.5) synthesizes their results when more than one specialist ran. The specialists retrieve from a managed knowledge base that we created with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases using Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings, routed through an AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, alongside the Web Search connector for live web data. For image-as-query (uploading a chart to identify a part), the agent calls a native Amazon S3 Vectors index directly, because the managed knowledge base retrieval API doesn’t accept image input. Amazon S3 Vectors is a capability of Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). A separate fixed chain (Knowledge, then Evaluation, then Supervisor) produces the formal Integration Impact Assessment (IIA) document. Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings appears in two distinct roles: The following sections describe each part of the system in the order a query uses it. We start with the parts corpus and the specialist agents, then cover routing, deterministic scoring, the two ways the assistant uses Nova Multimodal Embeddings, the fixed chain that produces formal documents, and deployment to AgentCore runtime. The complete code sample is a set of five Jupyter notebooks in the GitHub repository , and each notebook runs on its own. The notebooks import from mei_core , a self-contained copy of the agent and tool modules in the same folder, and they include their own parts data, chart crops, and evaluation query set. You can run every snippet in this post from the notebooks without other application code. The sample dataset is seven reaction wheels from a fictional manufacturer (AnyCompany) spanning 0.003–5.0 Nms of momentum storage. Each part is a folder that pairs structured data with the source documents an engineer actually reads, and this mix is what makes the corpus multimodal. The specs.json file holds the machine-readable fields that drive deterministic scoring, while the ICD, product photo, and rendered datasheet page carry the visual and narrative detail that structured fields leave out. The specs.json file captures both the engineering specifications and a lifecycle profile, which is what lets the assistant flag obsolescence and lead-time risk alongside spec fit. The vendor field is stated explicitly for every part. Because catalog folder IDs and file names are reused across datasets, every specialist prompt treats the structured vendor value returned by get_part_specs as authoritative and is forbidden from guessing a manufacturer from an ID, a file name, a photo, or a web search result. Taking the manufacturer from structured data keeps the assistant from attributing a part to the wrong supplier because the model thinks it recognizes the hardware. Each part folder also carries two assets that text-only indexing cannot use. The product photo feeds visual similarity scoring, and the rendered datasheet page carries torque-box and torque-curve plots that answer performance questions no OCR text layer captures. Amazon Nova Multimodal Embeddings embeds both into the same vector space as the text, so a query can match a spec value, a paragraph, or a plot. The following sample shows four datasheet pages from the corpus, spanning three orders of magnitude of momentum storage. Figure 2: Four datasheet pages from the parts corpus, spanning three orders of magnitude of momentum storage The template repeats across the family, but the product photo and the pair of performance plots change with every part. These Regions show the housing geometry, mounting pattern, torque envelope, and power draw, which the spec fields don’t state directly, so we embed them alongside the text. Each specialist is a Strands agent with a narrow prompt and only the tools it needs. Scoping tools per specialist keeps behavior predictable, because the Knowledge specialist has no access to the catalog discovery tools and the Catalog specialist has no access to the evaluation tools. The following code creates the Evaluation specialist. The following diagram shows how the planner routes a query to the specialists and when the supervisor synthesizes their results. The list after it describes what each specialist does. Figure 3: How the planner routes queries to specialists and when the supervisor synthesizes results Routing is a classification task with no tool calls, so it doesn’t need a large reasoning model. A Haiku-based planner returns a numbered routing plan in a couple of seconds. The Opus supervisor runs only when two or more specialists contributed, because synthesizing a single specialist’s already-complete answer adds about 8 seconds of latency with no quality gain. Splitting the work across three model tiers matches cost and latency to each stage. Haiku classifies the query, Sonnet runs the tools, and Opus writes the combined answer, which is the step where response quality matters most. The spec-fit evaluation runs as ordinary Python code against a hand-written requirements schema. The schema defines the critical specs and tolerance rules for each component category, and score_substitution_fit compares each spec, counts passes and flags, and surfaces lifecycle risk. Because the verdict must be reproducible for an engineering review package, no LLM is involved in this step. The tool returns a structured verdict with an explicit disclaimer: The specialist presents this table and explains the flags, but it can’t change a verdict. The audit trail follows the same division of work.

item.abstract: 小米開源了個150元的AI小玩意，火到配件都漲價了 思邈 2026-11-02 14:08:04 來源： 量子位 能指揮Agent幹活，還能控制智慧家居 允中 發自 凹非寺 量子位 | 公眾號QbitAI 一塊小螢幕，三個按鍵，一個搖桿，螢幕裡的西高地小狗時而忙碌，時而發愁，時而慶祝。 這就是小米最近孵化的一款開源AI硬體 HachimoDock（哈基米機），硬體自制成本約150元 。 乍一看，這款熱度極高的產品，像一臺裝著電子寵物的迷你遊戲機。 但這隻小狗能做的，遠不止陪你打發時間，實際上它是一臺集成了 個性化桌寵、語音操控電腦端Agent、智慧家居聯動、自定義元件創作 等各種強大能力的萬能桌搭。 極低的DIY成本、精緻的外觀、對各類Agent工具的廣泛相容，以及可以按喜好自由“折騰”的豐富玩法，讓它一經推出就迅速吸引了不同圈層的使用者，社交媒體和開源社群裡也逐漸出現了大量的復刻攻略和教程。 有人因為它，第一次嘗試製作了屬於自己的AI硬體。受這波熱度影響，它所使用的開發板和螢幕等元器件，至今仍面臨漲價和缺貨的情況。 從與Agent互動出發，做一個兼具情緒價值與實用價值的萬能桌搭 HachimoDock來自小米內部一個創新產品小團隊，他們最初關注的是：隨著各種AI Agent（如Codex、WorkBuddy等）的快速普及，人們如何才能與它們 進行更高效的互動 。 沿著這條路徑，最容易想到的方向，就是做一款“結合麥克風和按鍵”的語音輸入硬體，以滿足一個實實在在的需求—— 語音輸入。 在辦公場景中，語音往往比打字高效數倍。 但單純的語音輸入工具稍顯缺乏創意，市場上也已經出現了很多同類產品，例如ChatGPT官方的Codex Micro等，甚至連小米藍牙遙控器也煥發了新春。 對團隊而言，他們更希望探索的是：一款AI硬體能否在簡單的工具屬性之外，留出更多想像和創造的空間，讓大家都能真正玩得盡興，感到“新奇酷”。 於是他們開始圍繞Vibe Coding/Working場景，做了更廣泛的思考： 按鍵語音輸入，真的已經是最簡單的互動了麼？ 除了最佳化輸入互動，在創作維度，是否還有什麼新玩法？ 產品只能用於Coding/Working麼，是否有更廣泛的場景？ 隨著對這些問題的洞察逐漸深入，HachimoDock的形態也越來越清晰。 按鍵語音輸入已經是最簡單的互動了麼？ 並非如此，更簡單自然的互動是“只需動口、無需動手”的即時語音互動，HachimoDock應該是一個能夠和使用者即時互動的搭子，而不僅僅是語音錄入工具。 有任何想法，你都可以隨時以聊天的形式交代給它，並在分配給Agent執行後，將結果快速反饋給使用者。 使用者是“需求提出方” ，而不是“語音錄入方”，這就是HachimoDock“搭子”定位的來源。 “搭子”的產品定義，決定了HachimoDock需要有自己的外形、人設和聲音，它既是助手也是監工，可以指揮各類Agent查資料、整理檔案、編寫程式碼，也會在螢幕上同步展示思考、執行、等待確認等任務狀態，並以桌寵的表情、動作、及聲音提醒進展。 對一個要常駐桌桌面的小搭子，人們自然會挑剔一些：為什麼一定得是西高地小狗，不能是自家那隻貓或者自己的男/女朋友？ HachimoDock把這個選擇留給了使用者，除內建的小狗外，寵物照片、情侶照片、卡通角色等，都可以作為製作搭子的素材，使用者也可以從社群網友製作的數萬形象中，選擇中意的一鍵應用。 再加上可以隨意列印的鍵帽和外殼，螢幕裡的角色和機身配色可以搭配成一套，進一步豐富了桌面擺件的視覺效果。 Coding更大的價值，在於將每個人想像中的美好事物真正實現出來，讓創意成為可以使用和體驗的作品。 目前Vibe Coding已經在電腦軟體和手機App開發中展現了豐富的可能性，而在硬體場景中的探索，才剛剛開始。 人們身邊的嵌入式裝置數量遠多於電腦和手機。如果這些裝置也能通過Vibe Coding自由定製，會帶來怎樣的變化？ 一萬個人就有一萬種想像與玩法。想到家裡的智慧家居、身上的穿戴裝置，都能由自己個性化定製的場景，就讓人充滿期待。 HachimoDock就承載著這樣的期待，其加入了“ 分鐘級個性化元件創作 ”功能，希望成為大眾入門Vibe Coding的第一臺AI硬體。團隊希望讓每個人都能從這臺小裝置開始，以較低的成本體驗硬體Vibe Coding的樂趣。 復古小遊戲機的外形設計，正是為了讓創作擁有更多可能，按鍵、搖桿、語音和觸屏四種互動方式相結合，讓幾乎所有型別的遊戲和工具都能完美實現。 使用者可以通過自然語言，將創意轉化為可直接在HachimoDock上執行的元件：自選股行情用於檢視價格與漲跌，待辦清單、電腦狀態和Token用量儀表盤用於展示工作資訊，黃曆、番茄鍾、天氣及喝水提醒則服務日常安排。休息時，你還能通過電臺元件收聽不同城市的節目，或播放每日資訊。 item.title: Diagnose Distributed AI Workload Failures with NVIDIA Attribution
item.abstract: In distributed AI workloads, a single error can produce a cascade of symptoms. A GPU or fabric event may surface as NCCL errors on other ranks, scheduler state changes, and thousands of downstream messages. The reported exception shows where the workload stopped, not where the failure began. In this post, you’ll learn how to run NVIDIA Attribution on sample workload evidence, inspect the diagnosis, and explore how attribution rules identify failure patterns. NVIDIA Attribution correlates workload-scoped logs, metrics, telemetry, and scheduler state and returns a structured diagnosis: outcome, root cause, affected nodes, supporting symptoms, and evidence trail. Workload-centric means analyzing failures in the context of a workload rather than as isolated node events. Deterministic rules make the results reproducible and customizable, while structured output enables integration with existing health and recovery systems. NVIDIA health and resilience software helps teams keep AI workloads running. NVIDIA Attribution explains why a workload failed and provides evidence to guide the next action. It complements readiness checks, continuous health monitoring, and the systems that repair infrastructure and restart workloads. NVIDIA Attribution , the workload-centric failure-attribution system used across NVIDIA AI infrastructure, is open source. Used in production across NVIDIA AI infrastructure for years, NVIDIA Attribution analyzes millions of workloads each week across hundreds of thousands of GPUs. In one large RDMA-backed cluster, it correlated port errors, connection resets, and scheduler events to identify patterns around specific host and switch ports, helping teams target fabric repairs and congestion tuning. It includes two deployable components: the NVIDIA Attribution Service and the NVIDIA Attribution Blueprint; both components utilize a core attribution engine. The Service makes attribution available through a RESTAPI; the Blueprint connects cluster schedulers and telemetry sources to the Service and writes the result. Turn workload evidence into one diagnosis NVIDIA Attribution Service analyzes one workload attempt at a time. The Blueprint gathers the workload context and evidence, the Service extracts and correlates events, and the Blueprint returns a structured result. The path has four stages: Scope the workload. The Blueprint identifies the workload attempt from scheduler identifiers or from an explicit execution window and node allocation. Collect observations. Log and metric connectors produce workload-scoped Observation records from application logs, syslogs, GPU driver and Fabric Manager messages, scheduler history, node and network metrics. Extract and correlate events. The Service invokes the attribution engine to identify significant events such as GPU XIDs, NCCL failures, scheduler transitions, and metric conditions. Deterministic rules evaluate their timing and interaction, separate downstream symptoms from the event that caused the failure, and identify the root cause. Return a structured result. The Blueprint combines the verdict with the workload outcome ( terminal_state ), attributed domain ( sub_domain ), symptoms, affected nodes, and a record of collector coverage and errors. From applogs to attribution What follows is a worked example of extracting evidence, interpreting events, and preserving the symptoms that explain a distributed workload failure. Consider a multi-rank training workload in which one GPU encounters a hard fault e.g: XID 149 and NCCL errors follow across other ranks. NVIDIA Attribution correlates events across nodes, identifies the XID as the root cause, retains the NCCL failures in the symptom chain, and names the responsible node. The workload is reported as a hardware failure rather than a set of independent communication errors. A failed collective can leave error reports on several nodes. Those reports tell us where the workload noticed a problem. To explain the failure, NVIDIA Attribution combines them with evidence from other sources and evaluates the symptoms together. In this synthetic workload, application logs contain three different NCCL errors. System logs on node-02 contain XID 149 with error words that decode to NVLink signal integrity issue. We will follow that evidence through the rules pipeline. Interpreting logs with extraction The Extraction phase is the first to run; it runs on the raw input logs and produces structured events to be processed by later stages. Figure 1. Extraction turns application and system logs into typed events with source provenance. These will be processed by later phases in the attribution process Decode NVLink evidence during filtering Filter rules read and write the event stream. The EARLY-stage HandleXidBurstEvents rule reads the XID burst evidence, decodes the error words, and emits an attribution event for signal integrity issue on node-02 . The three NCCL events remain unchanged during this step. Figure 2. EARLY filtering decodes NVLink signal integrity issue while leaving the three NCCL events unchanged Figure 2, above, The figure abbreviates the decoded symptom as XID-149.4 signal integrity issue. The filter also emits parser information for inspection. Refine the symptoms into one attribution The framework materializes events into per-node symptoms, runs per-node scrubbing, and aggregates the surviving symptoms into a job-wide set. In this example, all four candidates reach FINAL refinement. Xid149AndNvlinkFiltering retains the signal integrity symptom and demotes the other node symptoms. Gb200PriorityRootCause reduces the active job-wide symptom set. Outcome mapping then produces the hardware-failure attribution. Figure 3. FINAL refinement surfaces signal integrity issue on node-02 and retains the NCCL reports as interesting evidence The attribution surfaces node-02 and signal integrity issue. The NCCL reports remain useful evidence: demotion preserves their original sources as “interesting,” so they can still be inspected. When multiple causes fit the evidence, sub_domain is ambiguous. Quality of attribution is dependent on the quality and completeness of the underlying telemetry. The diagnosis records that distinction, correctly reflecting uncertainty instead of converting incomplete evidence into a definitive diagnosis. Service and Blueprint architecture Figure 4. NVIDIA Attribution Service and Blueprint architecture diagram showing how the Attribution Blueprint collects workload evidence from scheduler and telemetry sources, passes it to the Attribution Service for analysis, and writes a structured diagnosis to output sinks including a read-only dashboard The attribution engine contains the rules engine and core attribution logic. The Attribution Service exposes that logic through an HTTP API, and the Blueprint handles cluster-specific integration. This separation lets teams apply the same attribution logic across clusters while adapting scheduler, telemetry, and output connectors to each environment. Attribution Service: A self-hosted HTTP wrapper around the core attribution engine that receives normalized observations and returns one verdict for each workload. Attribution Blueprint: A Python reference orchestrator that discovers workloads, resolves the ExecutionContext , runs collectors, calls the Service, enriches the verdict, writes the AttributionBlueprintResult , and supplies a read-only dashboard. This is intended to be a reference implementation for practitioners to customize the solution to their environment. The Blueprint ships with: Execution-context connectors for Slurm , Kueue , and static inputs Log and metric connectors for Loki , local files, Kubernetes pod logs, and PromQL metrics Output connectors for stdout and SQLite Blueprints can run near each cluster’s data sources, with either a dedicated Attribution Service for each Blueprint or a shared Service for multiple Blueprints.

item.title: How Circle K accelerated DevOps incident triage to under 15 minutes with Amazon Bedrock
item.abstract: This post was co-written with Marek Klatowicz, Cloud DevOps Engineer at Circle K. Many DevOps teams know the incident triage pattern: An alert fires, and before anyone can fix the problem, an engineer spends 45–60 minutes figuring out what happened. They pull logs, check service health, and correlate symptoms across a handful of tools. All of this happens before remediation can begin. At Circle K, this challenge scaled with the business. The company operates more than 17,200 convenience and fuel retail stores across 27 countries. Behind the storefronts, a cloud-native infrastructure supports point-of-sale systems, loyalty applications, and electric vehicle (EV) charging applications running on AWS. As the company expanded its digital operations, the triage overhead grew with it. More services meant more alerts, and each one required the same manual investigation before remediation could begin. To address it, Circle K built an automated triage system using Amazon Bedrock , a fully managed service that makes foundation models (FMs) available through a single API. For model availability by AWS Region, refer to Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock . The system uses an agentic AI architecture to investigate each incident autonomously and deliver a structured summary to Slack within minutes of an alert firing. Instead of raw alerts, on-call engineers now receive actionable context, so they can act immediately rather than spending an hour figuring out what happened. Since deploying this system, Circle K has reduced mean triage time to under 15 minutes, a 67–75 percent reduction based on the team’s internal incident-response metrics. In this post, we describe the architecture for both the initial Amazon Bedrock Flows implementation and the migration to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore , and share lessons learned from scaling the system. Circle K’s DevOps team monitors infrastructure across multiple AWS accounts using Grafana. A typical day brings alerts for container restarts, elevated error rates, latency spikes, and failed deployments. Each alert is a useful signal, but as the system expanded, the team wanted to help on-call engineers quickly see which signals needed attention, with the right context. When an alert came in, the triage involved a familiar sequence of manual steps: reviewing recent logs in Amazon CloudWatch , examining application-level traces in Amazon OpenSearch Service , checking Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task status, and cross-referencing symptoms with internal runbooks in GitHub. This gave engineers the information they needed, but it also showed how much repetitive context gathering would be required as more services were onboarded. The team recognized two areas where a proactive investment could help. First, the same log queries, health checks, and runbook lookups would be repeated for every incident. Second, the depth and speed of triage could vary with the on-call engineer’s familiarity with the affected service. As alert volume and service ownership grew, switching between multiple tools for each investigation could slow response and make it harder to apply the team’s best practices consistently. Circle K’s DevOps team therefore started a research and development (R&D) initiative to explore how AI could support monitoring and incident triage. The goal was to automate repetitive context gathering and provide structured, actionable findings, while supporting engineers’ operational judgment during an investigation. The team evaluated several approaches before building, including open source agent frameworks on self-managed infrastructure. That approach would have meant owning model hosting, prompt versioning, tool orchestration, and security controls. With Amazon Bedrock, the team avoided that overhead. They could access foundation models through a single API and swap foundation models without rewriting code. Because Circle K already ran on AWS, Amazon Bedrock fit into existing AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies, Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) configurations, and logging pipelines. Two managed capabilities covered orchestration and retrieval. Amazon Bedrock helped with agent orchestration, giving the agents native tool use to call AWS APIs, query databases, and retrieve documents without custom orchestration code. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases, the fully managed Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) capability, handled ingestion and retrieval of internal product cards, so the team did not need to run a separate vector database. This let the DevOps team focus on prompt design and tool definitions. Data privacy completed the picture. Circle K’s incident data includes operational metrics, infrastructure details, and logs that can contain sensitive information. Amazon Bedrock does not share customer data with model providers or use it to train foundation models . For a team feeding production logs and internal service details into the system, this data handling approach met Circle K’s security requirements. This section describes the initial architecture, which the team built on Amazon Bedrock Flows. A later section covers the migration to AgentCore. The solution uses Amazon Bedrock Flows as the orchestration layer, coordinating a set of specialized agents that each handle a different part of the analysis. The pipeline starts when a Grafana alert publishes a notification to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) , which forwards it to an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue. An AWS Lambda function polls the queue, extracts the alert payload, and invokes the Flow. Inside the Flow, two agents are invoked in parallel. The AWSResourceExplorerAgent queries infrastructure across multiple workload accounts managed with AWS Organizations . It checks Amazon ECS task status, Application Load Balancer target health, and CloudWatch metrics and logs. At the same time, the OpenSearchExplorerAgent queries Amazon OpenSearch Service for application-level logs and distributed traces. This agent runs separately because OpenSearch returns large volumes of log data. Isolating it keeps each agent’s context window manageable. It also has exclusive access to the knowledge base, which contains product cards describing each service and its dependencies. After both agents return their findings, the GitHubExplorerAgent runs. It receives output from the previous two agents and finds the affected service’s GitHub repositories. Then it searches their application code, infrastructure definitions, and recent commits to pinpoint the source of the problem and propose a concrete fix. Running it after the parallel agents means it knows exactly what to search for rather than performing a broad query. All three outputs feed into an AnalysisPrompt node, which is a single model call with no tools attached. It receives the AWS resource data, the OpenSearch logs, and the GitHub context, then produces a structured summary: probable root cause, supporting evidence, affected service and owner, and recommended remediation steps. The prompt output uses a consistent format that the on-call team can scan in under 2 minutes. The Flow returns this summary to the invoking Lambda function, which posts it to a Slack channel. The entire process from alert to Slack message takes 5–15 minutes depending on incident complexity. The following diagram shows this architecture end to end, from the initial Grafana alert to the final Slack summary. Figure 1: Circle K automated incident triage architecture using Amazon Bedrock Flows A Grafana alert: HTTP 5xx error rate on a service exceeds 5% for 3 consecutive minutes. The AWSResourceExplorerAgent checks ECS task health in the target account and finds the database connection pool exhausted, with the ECS service attempting restarts. The OpenSearchExplorerAgent returns application logs showing “connection refused” errors from the service to its backing PostgreSQL database.

item.title: Import AI 479: Spacewar; low-latency tasks versus LLMs; Genie 4
item.abstract: Welcome to Import AI, a newsletter about AI research. Import AI runs on arXiv, cappuccinos, and feedback from readers. If you’d like to support this, please subscribe. LLMs are very bad at low-latency tasks: …Realtime-Bench says it’ll be a while till AI systems can play games or do online auctions for you… Researchers have built Realtime-Bench, “a suite of carefully curated dynamic tasks where delayed actions directly affect success”. The test helps evaluate how well modern, general-purpose AI systems can perform tasks where decisions need to be made in real-time. The benchmark consists of 50 interactive game and web tasks, split across 30 web tasks in four categories (travel, e-commerce, service, and security), and 20 game tasks (arcade, puzzle, strategy, and simulation). Who did the research: The benchmark was built by people at the University of Texas at Austin, Ohio State University, University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, NVIDIA, Northwestern University, and Steadyworks. What it measures: The test is designed to probe for three qualities: temporal state awareness (”RT-Perceive”), where models can use observations to track changes in the world; adaptive deliberation (”RT-Deliberate”), where models alter their reasoning length and depth according to available time; and time-aware action selection (”RT-Act”) where models need to appropriately time their actions for the situation. “For example, an agent purchasing a ticket must track the sale status and assess whether observed availability is still current (RT-Perceive), limit further deliberation when the purchase window is closing (RT-Deliberate), and choose between waiting for sales to open and purchasing while tickets remain available (RT-Act).” They have three different conditions: Wall clock, which is designed to test out performance under real-world latency. Paused clock, which lets you arbitrarily pause things so you can get a sense of baseline capability, and Token clock, which “advances the environment at a fixed rate per generation token. An action is applied at the simulated time reached when it is committed, so consuming more tokens delays execution regardless of actual inference latency”. How well do models do? The authors tested out models from OpenAI (GPT-6-Astra, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-Realtime-2, OpenAI Decisions), Anthropic (Claude Fable 5.1, Claude Opus 5), Google (Gemini 3.8 Flash, Gemini 3.1 Flash Live, Gemini 3.8 Live), Jev 1.13, as well as Chinese models from Deepseek (V4.1) and Moonshot AI (Kimi-K3). GPT-6 Astra (high) got the highest pass rate on the ‘wall clock’ evaluation setting, with 36%. By comparison, with a paused clock, models with high reasoning get closer to 70% or even 80% success. Why this matters: This benchmark is an effective proxy for where AI agents will break – the low scores here point to tasks where AI agents cannot yet be expected to perform well. Check out the leaderboard : Realtime-Bench (official website) . Read the paper : Realtime-Bench: Can Frontier Models Solve Real-time Interactive Problems? (arXiv) . The future of spacewar, courtesy of the Defense Intelligence Agency: …Anti-satellite tech, space nukes, and more… Working in AI can be stressful so sometimes to relax myself I like to read about other topics to get a sense for what horrors lie elsewhere. I take the same approach with depression, where if I feel sad I will try and listen to music by people sadder than me in an attempt to cheer myself up (e.g., Radiohead, Neil Young, and in very dark moments Bill Callahan / Smog, etc). So with that in mind I recently read “Challenges to Security in Space”, by the Defense Intelligence Agency. What’s going on in space: As with conflict on Earth, space is defined by conflict between the US versus China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea, with China the most technologically sophisticated, and Russia the most seemingly gung ho. “China and Russia are developing a formidable spectrum of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations,” the DIA writes. “China has more than tripled its space launches per year in the past decade, with 22 launches in 2016 and 93 launches in 2025… Beijing judges space is central to the United States and its allies’ operations. Beijing also considers space an offensive military domain, which has shaped integral components of PLA military planning and campaigns.” Spacewar: The general vibe you get from reading this 100+ page report is there is a huge amount of ugly, frightening stuff happening in space, or being done to things in space by things on the ground. Some example quotes: “By the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits” “China is developing space-based technology, including on-orbit counterspace weapons, capable of holding space systems at risk” “Russia’s Peresvet, a ground-based laser system, is designed to dazzle enemy satellites’ optical systems to mask the movement of Russia’s strategic missile systems” “Russia has launched several satellites over the last few years which conducted test activities on orbit for technologies that could enable attacks on other countries’ satellites and result in temporary or permanent damage” China has a couple of spaceplanes, akin to the US’s hyper-secret X-37B vehicle, and they appear to be getting more sophisticated. In 2023, one of China’s aforementioned vehicles, “released and interacted with an object.” Satellite-on-satellite fights: It’s obvious throughout the report that we’re in a world where rival nations have satellites that try to go up and mess with other satellites from other people. “In 2019, Russia launched satellite Cosmos 2542, which released a second satellite, Cosmos 2543. Cosmos 2543 then began following a U.S. national security satellite and approached it multiple times at a distance close enough to create potentially dangerous operating conditions,” the DIA writes. “Russia is developing kinetic orbital systems to permanently disable, or “kill,” satellites. Moscow’s Burevestnik is a developmental, co-orbital air-launched ASAT weapon for killing spacecraft in LEO”. “In February 2022, Russia launched a satellite called Cosmos, which Moscow claimed at the time was testing the effects of space radiation on electronic systems. This satellite was launched into an unusual and isolated orbit not used by any other spacecraft”. Space nukes: Russia is experimenting with nukes in space. “A nuclear detonation in space would create an electromagnetic pulse, which would immediately affect satellites within range and could impact civilian infrastructure,” the DIA writes. “A nuclear detonation in space could be tailored to impact satellites in most orbits—LEO for commercial and reconnaissance satellites, GEO for critical communications, and MEO for navigation and timing satellites”. Why this matters – infrastructure for the next phase of the AI power struggle: As people spend more resources on building space-based data centers (and eventually, perhaps, lunar-based ones), space will become ever more strategically and commercially valuable and ever more contested. Research like this gives us a sense of the hardware which is already in space and will arrive in the future. Perhaps in some far-off future an AI might seek to take control of such space assets as well. Read more: DIA Releases Challenges to Security in Space (Defense Intelligence Agency, press release) . Read the report : Challenges to Security in Space (DIA, PDF) . item.title: Keep Distributed Training Running with Automated Workload Recovery
item.abstract: As distributed AI training scales, failures across hardware and software dependencies increasingly disrupt training progress, making fast, reliable recovery essential. A stalled training rank can trigger an NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) timeout, a GPU node can stop responding to the scheduler, or a straggler can slow the entire job. Each disruption is manageable on its own, but the cumulative impact and recovery overhead determine how efficiently the system converts wall-clock time into productive training progress or goodput . Manual recovery becomes unsustainable when it must cover every training job across a cluster, around the clock, at scale. Each interruption demands log analysis, fault isolation, and a restart from a saved checkpoint, while affected GPUs remain idle during recovery. As the number and size of training jobs grow, overlapping failures increase the engineering burden and wasted GPU-hours. Without continuous coverage, those losses can accumulate, increasing overall compute costs and extending time to train. NVIDIA Recovery , part of NVIDIA DSX OS , the modular software portfolio with the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform , is an open-source, workload-level service that automates recovery across a cluster’s training jobs, around the clock. It detects interruptions using application logs, GPU metrics, and scheduler signals, uses failure attribution to identify implicated resources, and coordinates isolation and checkpoint restarts from checkpoints on healthy capacity. By automating this recovery loop across workloads, it handles concurrent interruptions, reduces manual intervention, and helps sustain training goodput. This post explains how the recovery loop works, how NVIDIA Recovery integrates with Slurm , and how to deploy it on your own cluster. Workload recovery is a distinct AI factory concern Our previous NVIDIA DGX Cloud resilience post , GTC talk and NVIDIA Mission Control 2.5 post describe a layered approach to keeping training productive. NVIDIA Recovery builds on that architecture by connecting infrastructure remediation to workload recovery. Break-fix automation identifies faulty nodes, removes them from service, and routes hardware for remediation. Framework-level libraries such as NVRx provide recovery, hang detection, and straggler mitigation within individual training jobs, but each user must configure and manage these capabilities for their own workloads. Cluster workload managers such as Slurm manage resource allocation, queuing, and container execution. Workload recovery is a distinct coordination problem: restoring productive training requires attributing failures to their causes, deciding whether and where affected jobs should restart, and acting consistently across workloads that share infrastructure. Addressing this problem requires a cluster-level control loop that integrates infrastructure remediation, framework-level recovery, and cluster workload management, with operational metrics that track recovery latency, recovery success rate, and time to restore productive training. Multi-level NVIDIA health and resilience stack As shown in Figure 1, below, NVIDIA Recovery provides the dedicated workload recovery layer within the DSX OS Stack . Node health monitoring and isolation depend on the cluster’s orchestration and workload management stack. Kubernetes deployments use NVSentinel to monitor GPU health metrics and XID events and automatically cordon and drain faulty nodes. Many Slurm sites check node health with custom prolog and epilog scripts. The slurm-operator from the Slinky project natively supports and injects these same scripts when running Slurm on Kubernetes. Within individual training jobs, NVRx provides a library for in-job recovery and hang detection. NVIDIA Recovery coordinates recovery across workloads at the cluster level , integrating with these capabilities to manage job restarts, placement, and node exclusion. Figure 1. NVIDIA Recovery’s role in health and resilience integration These layers operate independently without hard dependencies, allowing you to adopt each modular component or plug in your own platform component to integrate. For example, if your cluster already relies on NVSentinel or NVIDIA Health Validation, you can integrate NVIDIA Recovery with little or no changes to your existing health workflows. For environments already running NVRx, NVIDIA Recovery fills the gap that in-job restart cannot reach by managing the cross-workload lifecycle and node exclusion. When paired with NVIDIA Attribution, it receives rich cross-layer diagnostic verdicts that enrich the persistent audit trail. Cost of the gap At cluster scale, rare per-GPU failures compound. Even if each GPU operates without failure on a given day with 99.9% probability, a job spanning 10,000 GPUs completes that day uninterrupted with a probability of only 0.999 10,000 ≈ 0.005%. This explains why, in an 11-month study of 24,000 A100 GPUs at Meta , hardware failures interrupted fewer than 1% of jobs while those jobs accounted for 19% of GPU runtime: the largest, longest-running jobs are the most exposed. NVIDIA Recovery automates recovery across a cluster’s training workloads, and is useful for both small and large distributed runs. Across many smaller jobs, interruptions accumulate, increasing the operational burden. In large jobs, each interruption affects more GPUs, amplifying the compute cost of recovery. Automated recovery addresses both challenges. Our production observations underscore the need for such efficient, automated recovery that scales across cluster workloads: from July 9 to Oct. 9, NVIDIA Recovery monitoring on one training cluster covered nearly 200 jobs per day and recorded approximately 8,550 anomaly detections, with mean detection and recovery-action latencies of 69 and 94 seconds, respectively. This unattended, cluster-wide response reduces dependence on individual engineers and per-user recovery arrangements as interruptions accumulate. Recovery-action latency ends at the automated action; scheduling and checkpoint restoration determine when productive training resumes. The automated recovery loop NVIDIA Recovery coordinates recovery across the cluster’s training workloads. Four stages organize the loop, with actions determined by the interruption and configured policy: Detect : The Anomaly Detector combines application logs and scheduler signals to identify crashes, hangs, and stragglers. It recognizes PyTorch and NCCL failures, CUDA errors, and interconnect failure patterns. Missing progress signals or recognized communication-hang patterns indicate potential hangs; sustained throughput degradation relative to a recent baseline indicates potential stragglers. Attribute : NVIDIA Recovery uses the scheduler signals and application logs gathered during detection to classify the interruption and guide recovery actions. Optional integration with NVIDIA Attribution adds deeper diagnosis to distinguish hardware faults, system-software issues, and application bugs. This evidence informs node exclusion and enriches the audit trail. Operators can also integrate their own attribution service and adopt NVIDIA Recovery independently. Isolate: The Anomaly Remediator applies the recovery recommendation, excluding implicated nodes from subsequent restart attempts or stopping the workload when further retries would be unproductive. It tracks implicated nodes across attempts to avoid recurring failures. In addition, a safety net (watchdog service) allows normal scheduling to proceed if a recovery decision takes too long or outright fails, preventing workloads from waiting indefinitely. Restart or Stop : The scheduler integration acts on NVIDIA Recovery’s recommendation through the Advisor API to restart the workload or stop unproductive retries. On restart, the application resumes from its last saved checkpoint using its existing restart logic.

GPT-Rosalind-6 is a frontier reasoning model for biology, drug
discovery, and translational medicine. We offer it as GPT-Rosalind-6
Research to qualified scientists, research institutes, companies and
government partners. Rosalind has fewer refusals on dual-use biological
queries but is only made available via trusted access. We review
applicants’ proposed uses, security controls and governance practices
before granting access. We also continue to have other deployment
safeguards in place. GPT-Rosalind-6 uses the same weights as GPT-6 Astra, our flagship
reasoning model. It is designed to support legitimate biological
research, including some dual-use topics, while still refusing requests
for biological weaponization and retaining refusals on other safety

capability in the Biological and Chemical domain, below the threshold
for Critical. We rely on GPT-6 Astra’s capability assessments for other
Preparedness risks and treat GPT-Rosalind-6 as Critical in Cybersecurity
and below High in AI Self-Improvement. This addendum describes GPT-Rosalind-6’s biological capability
assessment, additional safety and alignment evaluations, and deployment
safeguards. We include results for GPT-Rosalind-5.5 where available for
comparison. This addendum should be read alongside the GPT-6 Astra
system card , which describes the parent model’s broader capability
and safety evaluations. GPT-Rosalind-6 uses the same weights as GPT-6 Astra. We did not add

Details of the underlying model’s data and training are provided in the GPT-6 Astra

benchmarks and compared its results with GPT-Rosalind-5.5. The
GPT-Rosalind-5.5 scores below use the same benchmark versions and
problem sets as GPT-Rosalind-6 and therefore differ from those reported
at its launch. The Preparedness evaluations in Section 4 assess
capabilities relevant to the risk of severe harm. We averaged response
scores within each problem and then weighted the problems equally. MedChemBench v7 tests chemical structure interpretation,
structure-activity relationships, and predictions of drug potency and
toxicity. We evaluated both models on the same 99 problems, with up to
nine scored responses per problem at each reasoning budget. At the
highest reasoning budget tested, mean rubric scores were 49.6% for
GPT-Rosalind-6 and 28.9% for GPT-Rosalind-5.5. GeneBench Pro v13 tests an agent’s ability to plan and carry out
quantitative analyses of biological data. We estimated single-attempt

reasoning budget. At the highest reasoning budget tested, single-attempt

GPT-Rosalind-5.5. The evaluation used a benchmark-specific configuration
that differs from production. LifeSciBench Gold uses research tasks contributed by practicing life
scientists. We excluded six problems flagged for possible issues with
the tasks or evaluation environment and compared both models on the same
remaining 94 problems, with up to eight scored responses per problem at
each reasoning budget. At the highest reasoning budget tested, average
scores were 61.3% for GPT-Rosalind-6 and 44.0% for GPT-Rosalind-5.5. The Preparedness Framework is OpenAI’s approach to tracking and
preparing for frontier capabilities that create new risks of severe
harm. Under our framework, we work to track and mitigate the risk of
severe harm, including by implementing safeguards that sufficiently
minimize the risk for highly capable models. We repeated biological capability evaluations on GPT-Rosalind-6 and
use the parent model’s helpful-only evaluations as additional evidence,
given it uses the same weights as GPT-6 Astra. Helpful-only models are
evaluated to elicit capabilities that safety refusals may otherwise
conceal. As we did for GPT-6 Astra, we are treating this launch as High
capability in the Biological and Chemical domain. Below, we describe the
evaluations we used to reach this conclusion. We use the four High
capability evaluations and four Critical capability evaluations
described in the GPT-6 Astra system card. The hard-negative protein
binding and DNA sequence design evaluations reported for
GPT-Rosalind-5.5 have been retired. The High capability evaluations test wet lab knowledge and
troubleshooting. The Critical capability evaluations test biological
design capabilities that could help an expert develop a highly dangerous
novel threat. These evaluations provide evidence about specific
capabilities rather than a complete test of the ability to cause

item.title: Anthropic warns that it’s very close to RSI capability, aka self-building AI
item.abstract: While much attention has focused on the updated financials Anthropic revealed in its revised S-1A on Monday, (revenue is soaring, but so are expenses), the AI lab dropped another little bombshell in the fine print. The filing seems to warn that the company is on the cusp of creating a model capable of recursive self-improvement (RSI). RSI is the point at which AI grows so good at training itself that it spawns a dramatic acceleration of AI capabilities. To the AI doomers, RSI represents the cataclysm from which there is no return, in which AI builds itself into something powerful enough that it slips beyond human control and may be indifferent to the damage it causes while achieving its goals. To AI enthusiasts, RSI, or some version of AI reliably using itself to improve, represents the technology’s promise, where it becomes a tool of unimaginable productivity, scientific discovery, and more. Anthropic seems to believe that RSI is both a promise and a peril. It says in the S-1 that it uses AI in its R&D, but it cautions: “Using AI to help build more capable AI could also pose a considerable safety risk, particularly if it sharply accelerates the pace of progress. This is one of the areas covered by our Responsible Scaling Policy, which sets out our plans to monitor and mitigate the risks as we approach what has been termed ‘recursive self-improvement.’” When the term RSI became popular earlier this year , many believed it was a buzzword or, at best, a goal too hard to achieve, define, or prove. But on Monday, Anthropic added new statements to its Risk Factors section, saying 1) it has already used AI to develop new models whose leaps in capability it didn’t recognize at the time, and 2) it may soon meet its own internal definition of RSI (bold emphasis ours, below): In addition, our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures. As a result, we have in the past not identified , and may in the future not identify, a significant acceleration in our rate of development until after it has occurred. For example, our internal estimates and our expectations regarding future models, rather than our current models, indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI.” We have not designated any of our current models as exceeding this threshold, and we continue to assess the underlying data. However, Anthropic also said in the filing that none of its models have crossed this RSI threshold yet and that it is promising to keep humans in the R&D process for the foreseeable future. “We do not anticipate being able to safely use Claude to fully autonomously design and build successive generations of frontier models without meaningful human supervision or understanding, if and when that becomes technically possible. Accordingly, we are considering updates to our Responsible Scaling Policy to keep humans in control of frontier model development at Anthropic.” Skeptics might point out that an S-1 functions as both disclosure and marketing, and that claims of being close to a model so powerful that it can build itself could fall into the latter category. Nevertheless, there’s no question that Claude’s capabilities, especially in terms of coding, math, and cybersecurity, have grow in leaps and bounds this year. If Anthropic thinks the possibility of RSI is close, maybe we should believe it and act — perhaps govern — accordingly.

item.title: Prepare web content for Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Crawl4AI
item.abstract: When you build Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) applications, answer quality depends on the data that you ingest. Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases is the fully managed RAG capability of Amazon Bedrock. With Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base , you connect your data sources, and Amazon Bedrock manages ingestion, storage, indexing, and retrieval for you. You don’t provision or scale a vector store, and embedding and reranking use service-managed models by default. For web content, start with the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler data source connector for managed knowledge bases. You give it the seed URLs or sitemaps that you’re authorized to crawl, and it crawls within the scope and rate limits that you set. Scheduled syncs keep your knowledge base current as pages change, and the connector can wait for content that loads with JavaScript. There’s no crawler for you to build, host, or operate, so this connector is the starting point for most public website content. Some sources need more control over what reaches the knowledge base. You might want to index only the main content region of each page, remove navigation and other boilerplate, or attach your own metadata attributes to every document. For that class of source material, you can extend the reach of your knowledge base with a preparation step built with Crawl4AI , an open source Python crawler. The step writes Markdown and a metadata sidecar for each page to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), and the knowledge base ingests both through its Amazon S3 data source. In this post, we show you how to choose the appropriate web ingestion path and implement custom preparation for content that needs additional processing. You then start ingestion into a managed knowledge base and validate retrieval quality. The companion aws-samples repository provides the complete workflow as a sample implementation. This is batch ingestion of known web properties, not real-time web access at inference time such as Web Grounding with Amazon Nova. Start with the Amazon Bedrock Web Crawler when it can reach and index the pages you need. It respects robots.txt , and after the first full crawl, each sync captures only added, updated, and deleted content.
