item.title: I Am the Reason OpenAI Is Killing Unlimited Chats
item.abstract:
I Am the Reason OpenAI Is Killing Unlimited Chats Okay, probably not. But after what I've been doing with ChatGPT, I can understand why they might want to. OpenAI recently announced changes that will kill unlimited ChatGPT chats and merge it with Codex usage. The unlimited chats I'd been using for development won't work quite the same way. For the past few months, I've essentially been doing all my software development using unlmited ChatGPT conversations without burning through my Codex limits. It started with MCP ChatGPT's support for custom MCP servers and OpenAI's Secure MCP Tunnel meant I could expose tools running on my own machines directly to regular ChatGPT conversations. So I started experimenting. I built a unified MCP server that runs on my Windows laptop, with a similar setup on my VPS, and integrated a few open-source projects: Desktop Commander: Gives ChatGPT the ability to access files and folders, read and write code, execute terminal commands, run tests, and manage processes. CUA (Computer Use Agent): Adds computer-use capabilities, including screenshots, mouse interactions, clicking buttons, inspecting visual elements, and testing browser or desktop applications. The MCP tools exposed to a regular ChatGPT conversation. Suddenly ordinary ChatGPT converssations could do most of the practical development work I previously used Codex for. They could inspect repositories, modify code, run commands, debug errors, and visually verify their changes. Connecting everything through OpenAI's tunnel The next challenge was making my local MCP servers accessible to ChatGPT. OpenAI provides a Secure MCP Tunnel, which turned out to be exactly what I needed. I connected my unified MCP gateway through the tunnel, authenticated the connection using an API key, and exposed my MCP tools directly to ChatGPT. No custom cloud infrastructure was needed just to bridge ChatGPT to my laptop. The tunnel and MCP integrations didn't require separate paid API inference calls. I used open-source tools, OpenAI's provided tunnel tooling, my existing ChatGPT subscription, and computers I already had. OpenAI Secure MCP Tunnel and local MCP setup ChatGPT chats connect to a local unified MCP gateway through an OpenAI Secure MCP Tunnel. The gateway routes tools to Desktop Commander and Enhanced TryCua. 01 / CONNECTION ARCHITECTURE One private MCP connection, multiple local capabilities. ChatGPT Regular conversations Secure MCP Tunnel OpenAI-hosted tunnel-client Runs on my computer tool calls HTTPS local MCP process Unified MCP gateway Node.js router / tool aggregation Desktop Commander Files · code · terminal · tests Enhanced TryCua Screen · mouse · browser · UI Local backend tools can also be hosted on my VPS. Connection architecture. I improved the integration Of course, once I got everything working, I couldn't resist tinkering with the tools themselves. I made several enhancements to the CUA integration to improve how ChatGPT interacted with my computer and how results appeared inside conversations. One example was getting actual screenshots to render directly inside ChatGPT . Instead of receiving a screenshot tool result that ChatGPT could inspect but I couldn't easily see, I added support for displaying captured screenshots through a custom MCP App viewer. I also improved how tool-call results were handled, making them easier for me to read within ChatGPT chats Custom MCP enhancements Open-source Desktop Commander and TryCua are extended with inline screenshot display, reliable tool responses, and dashboard monitoring. 03 / MY ENHANCEMENTS Small additions to make the underlying tools practical. Base MCP tools Desktop Commander · CUA Screenshot viewer Captured screen visible inside ChatGPT Reliable tool results Image bounds · consistent errors Monitoring and controls Live logs · health · CPU / RAM Better UX Real workflows Custom tool integrations. My fun little AI development workflow Since ChatGPT chats cannot spawn or control subchats/subganets so I had to be a bit creative in order to do multi-agent development and orchestration. Parallel AI software development workflow Premium model creates plan, issues are assigned to several ChatGPT workers, which share access to MCP tools. 02 / WORKFLOW Premium planning. Independent GitHub issues. Multiple Sol High workers. Astra / Pro model System design and planning GitHub issues Small, scoped tasks Parallel worker pool Separate ChatGPT conversations Sol High · Chat A Issue 1 Sol High · Chat B Issue 2 Sol High · Chat C Issue 3 Sol High · Chat D Issue 4 Shared MCP access Read · edit · run tests · inspect results Planning and parallel execution. I'd start with a more capable reasoning model, such as Astra in Codex or the limited Pro model in ChatGPT, and use it to create a detailed implementation plan. Next, I'd ask it to break the plan into smaller, well-defined GitHub issues. Each issue contained enough context, requirements, and acceptance criteria that another AI agent could pick it up independently. Essentially, I was turning a large development task into a queue of smaller jobs. Then I'd open several separate ChatGPT conversations, each running Sol 6 High, and assign them different issues. Because all those chats had access to my MCP server, they could actually work on the code. They could read the project, edit files, run tests, inspect errors, and iterate until their assigned task was complete. And at the time, I could use Sol High chats without hitting the kind of usage limits I encountered in Codex. Sure, Sol High was slower than the premium models, but when usage was effectively unlimited, I was willing to put up with it. I'd have multiple conversations working on separate tasks, while saving my more limited premium model usage for architecture, difficult decisions, and reviews. It wasn't perfect. Parallel agents sharing a filesystem need coordination, and occasionally an issue would require a stronger model to intervene. But for well-defined coding tasks, it worked surprisingly well. I was essentially using ChatGPT as a pool of coding agents, with GitHub issues acting as the task queue. I even built a dashboard for it My Windows MCP supervisor dashboard, showing connection health and recent tool calls. I also built a super lightweight interface where I can start or stop the entire MCP connection, monitor server health, track CPU and memory usage, and inspect a live feed of tool calls. I can see when ChatGPT reads a file, executes a command, or invokes a computer-use tool. The dashboard also tracks failures and lets me inspect recent activity. OpenAI has now killed unlimited chats As like all good things, this must also come to an end. I am sad that this is now going away. Unlimited chats was the only thing holding me back to an OpenAI sub. I personally prefer the Claude models greatly and I am going to jump ship. Claude Opus in particular seems to be much smarter for my use cases and I also get more mileage out of a Claude sub vs a Codex sub. To be clear, I am not breaking any rules. I am simply making the best use of what OpenAI has made available to me: ChatGPT conversations, MCP support, secure tunnels, and the ability to connect my own tools. Of course, I don't seriously think my setup had anything to do with OpenAI's decision. And although I am sad about not having unlimited chats anymore, but I am still glad about the extra usage i was able to squeeze out of my sub. So, OpenAI, if you're reading this: I'm not sorry about that. Claude here i come.

item.title: China's First Frontier AI Export Controls: Mofcom Announcement No. 48

Authors: Cloud Security Alliance AI Safety Initiative Published: 2026-10-23 Categories: AI Governance and Regulation Download PDF Download Markdown China’s First Frontier AI Export Controls: MOFCOM Announcement No. 48 Key Takeaways On October 16, 2026, China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) issued Announcement No. 48 of 2026. The announcement proposes adding 40 technologies to the Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited or Restricted from Export , 23 of them in artificial intelligence, and it imposes an interim pre-export registration requirement that is already in effect [1][2]. China’s catalogue has touched AI before: the 2020 revision added personalized recommendation and AI interaction interface technology [6]. Unlike those 2020 additions, the draft reaches frontier model weights, agent architectures, and AI-enabled offensive cyber capability, with explicit technical thresholds for each [1]. The announcement contains two instruments with different legal status. The catalogue additions are a draft open for comment until November 15, 2026, while the registration requirement applies now, including to exports that have started but are not yet complete [1][2]. Within the draft, model weights are restricted at frontier scale. Weights, key checkpoints, source code, architecture, and training and inference optimization know-how are restricted if a model meets any one of three tests: at least 10^26 FLOPs of training compute, at least 2 trillion parameters, or a global top-10 position on public evaluation rankings, global call volume, or comparable measures at the time of export [1][3]. Agents are controlled independently of the model. Planning, multi-agent coordination, tool use, and game-theoretic decision technologies are restricted above set benchmarks, and high-performance agents built for critical infrastructure, defense, or core government use are prohibited outright [1]. The line between service access and custody determines most enterprise exposure. MOFCOM says API, app, web, SaaS, and lightweight on-device use do not count as exporting a large model. Deploying a restricted model locally outside China does count, though automatic licensing may apply on a Chinese company’s own overseas cloud [2]. Multinationals also face exposure through licensing deals and changes of ownership or control, not only through product exports, and analysts read the registration form as potentially capturing intra-group code sharing as well [2][3][4]. Any transfer of ownership, licensing for overseas use, or shift of control to a foreign entity can trigger registration [2][4]. Background China regulates outbound technology transfer under two overlapping regimes. The first is the technology-trade regime under the Foreign Trade Law and the Regulations on Technology Import and Export Administration, which governs the catalogue being revised here. The second is the dual-use export-control regime under the 2020 Export Control Law [5]. MOFCOM’s spokesperson described the revision as routine and grounded in Article 20 of the Foreign Trade Law. The spokesperson stressed that it “does not target any specific country, region, or entity” and that the aim is to prevent uncontrolled diffusion while protecting legitimate cooperation [2]. The catalogue has been revised several times since 2001. The August 2020 revision, which added recommendation-algorithm technology, coincided with the proposed sale of TikTok to a U.S. buyer and was reported as likely to complicate that deal [3][6]. Across all three sectors, Announcement No. 48 proposes 14 prohibited and 26 restricted items: 23 in AI, 5 in biomedicine, and 12 in photovoltaics [2]. In China’s technology-trade framework, prohibited technologies may not be exported at all, while restricted technologies require a license from commerce and science authorities. ChinaTalk notes that licensing is administered by provincial authorities, although central authorities have intervened in prominent cases [3]. The official annex groups the AI items into large models, agents, compute clusters, chip design, and information-processing technologies. It also excludes from management any technology that has already entered the public domain through open-source release or academic publication [1]. The interim registration requirement is the part that applies today. From the announcement date until the revised catalogue takes effect, exporters must register through MOFCOM’s unified business platform before exporting any listed technology. Registration covers four triggers: transfer of technology ownership abroad, licensing of domestic technology for overseas use, a change in ownership or control that makes a foreign entity the owner or controller, and other cases MOFCOM designates [2][4]. Exporters must decide for themselves whether a technology falls within scope. The registration form asks for recipient details, destination, technology description, end use, and estimated value [2][4]. The timing also matters for enterprises that already track U.S. controls. CSA’s prior research documented the first U.S. use of export-control authority to suspend a broadly deployed commercial frontier model [9]. Announcement No. 48 means frontier AI supply chains now face formal outbound controls from both of the largest AI-producing jurisdictions. ChinaTalk observes that the 10^26 FLOP threshold mirrors the figure used in the 2023 U.S. executive order and the since-rescinded 2025 U.S. AI Diffusion rule. The authors also estimate that no released Chinese model currently exceeds it [3]. Security Analysis What the AI Annex Actually Controls The annex is granular, and its structure matters for scoping. item.title: Support New AI Frameworks Faster Using NVIDIA Workload Map
item.abstract:
NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform brings together technologies to help the ecosystem design, build, and operate more efficient AI factories, including open source, modular software components built to support multi-tenant operations and scaling. Operating an AI factory requires a shared understanding of distributed workloads: their components, pod templates, replica counts, and status. On Kubernetes, each framework encodes that information differently. JobSet, LeaderWorkerSet, and other custom resources often require separate adapters before a tool can interpret and manage them. NVIDIA Workload Map provides a common description of Kubernetes workload structure that users can reuse across frameworks. As part of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform, Workload Map enables integrated schedulers, controllers, and platforms to interpret supported workload types without maintaining separate framework-specific parsing code. This post shows how to describe a distributed JobSet workload once, then reuse that definition for workload inspection, gang scheduling, and platform visibility. Why every workload type needs its own adapter On Kubernetes, a real workload is rarely a single pod. A distributed training job or a multi-node inference server is a small tree of resources: groups of pods, each with a role, a replica count, a pod template, and a status that depends on the workload type. Teams building schedulers, controllers, dashboards, or cost tools that must work across these workloads encounter this immediately. The NVIDIA Run:ai team faced the same challenge while creating its platform. For each new custom resource definition (CRD), developers answer the same questions in code: What’s the structure of the workload type? How is the resource’s status interpreted as a phase? How is the pod spec changed without breaking the workload? A developer answers those questions once per workload type and produces a per-CRD adapter. Each new framework a customer brings requires another adapter. That makes adapter development a roadmap item per framework, not a one-time cost, which is why support for a new workload type so often waits for a release. The following manifest shows a distributed training job as a user submits it: a JobSet with a leader Job and two worker Jobs, each with a pod requesting four GPUs. apiVersion: jobset.x-k8s.io/v1alpha2
kind: JobSet
metadata: name: demo
spec: replicatedJobs: - name: leader replicas: 1 template: spec: parallelism: 1 completions: 1 template: spec: containers: - name: leader image: ghcr.io/example/trainer:latest resources: limits: nvidia.com/gpu: 4 - name: worker replicas: 2 template: spec: parallelism: 1 completions: 1 template: spec: containers: - name: worker image: ghcr.io/example/trainer:latest resources: limits: nvidia.com/gpu: 4 The manifest describes one leader, two workers, and a total request of 12 GPUs. Interpreting that structure requires JobSet-aware code; kubectl lists the resources separately. Figure 1. kubectl lists the demo JobSet, its three Jobs, and their pods as separate resource entries $ kubectl get jobset,jobs,pods
NAME TERMINALSTATE RESTARTS COMPLETED SUSPENDED AGE
jobset.jobset.x-k8s.io/demo 0 3m46s NAME STATUS COMPLETIONS DURATION AGE
job.batch/demo-leader-0 Running 0/1 3m46s 3m46s
job.batch/demo-worker-0 Running 0/1 3m46s 3m46s
job.batch/demo-worker-1 Running 0/1 3m46s 3m46s NAME READY STATUS RESTARTS AGE
pod/demo-leader-0-0-ksb4l 1/1 Running 0 3m47s
pod/demo-worker-0-0-qv955 1/1 Running 0 3m47s
pod/demo-worker-1-0-5smfn 1/1 Running 0 3m47s Owner references connect the Jobs to their JobSet, but a platform still needs a definition to interpret their roles and aggregate resource requests. Figure 2. NVIDIA Run:ai displays the component Jobs as three separate workloads, each requesting four GPUs, before the JobSet definition is registered Without a shared workload description, users must reconstruct the workload and total its GPU requests themselves. A common description of Kubernetes workload structure Workload Map (formerly Karta; the CRD’s resource kind remains Karta) ships as a Kubernetes CRD plus a Go library that interprets workload definitions. Each definition specifies where to find pod templates, replica counts, and status fields for its workload type. Workload Map supplies a shared structural view to scheduling and platform consumers. KAI Scheduler uses its definitions to interpret pod grouping and gang-scheduling instructions, while NVIDIA Run:ai uses them for workload management and visibility. Each consumer acts on the same description, reducing the need for separate framework-specific parsers. The Go library resolves a live object into a uniform structural view. With a workload definition in hand, a consumer can: Extract pod templates, replica counts, status, and metadata. Update pod specs, labels, and annotations across every instance. Understand the workload hierarchy, for example, a JobSet’s replicated Jobs and their pods. Workload Map includes a catalog of prebuilt, tested definitions for JobSet, PyTorchJob, RayCluster, RayJob, RayService, KServe, Knative, MPIJob, NVIDIA NIM, LeaderWorkerSet, Milvus, Grove PodCliqueSet , and NVIDIA Dynamo . Additional workload types can be added by writing a YAML definition that describes their structure and status. The key is that workload knowledge moves out of compiled adapters and into data developers can write, review, and apply to a cluster like any other manifest. The rest of this post describes the JobSet example, then shows how the same definition supports workload inspection, gang scheduling, and platform visibility. Writing a workload definition for JobSet A workload definition, expressed as a Workload Map resource, describes that shape. The following excerpt shows key parts of the JobSet definition. The full version ships in the repository . The root component defines the workload’s own kind and how its status is read. apiVersion: run.ai/v1alpha1
kind: Karta
spec: structureDefinition: rootComponent: name: jobset kind: group: jobset.x-k8s.io version: v1alpha2 kind: JobSet statusDefinition: conditionsDefinition: path: .status.conditions statusMappings: running: - byExpression: expression: "(.status.replicatedJobsStatus // []) | any(.ready > 0 and .active > 0) and all(.failed == 0)" expectedResult: "true" completed: - byConditions: - type: Completed status: "True" failed: - byConditions: - type: Failed status: "True" statusMappings is the translation layer. JobSet does not report a plain “Running” condition, so the definition derives it with a jq expression over replicatedJobsStatus (any Job ready and active, none failed) and maps the native Completed and Failed conditions onto the shared vocabulary a consumer already uses. When a RayJob or a LeaderWorkerSet is described, its very different status maps to the same categories. The next excerpt defines the child component: the structure inside the workload. childComponents: - name: replicatedjob kind: { group: batch, version: v1, kind: Job } ownerRef: jobset specDefinition: podTemplateSpecPath: .spec.replicatedJobs[].template.spec.template scaleDefinition: replicasPath: .spec.replicatedJobs[] | .replicas * .template.spec.parallelism instanceIdPath: .spec.replicatedJobs[].name A JobSet declares its roles as a list, so .spec.replicatedJobs holds one entry per role. The [] in these paths means “for each entry in that list,” and each entry is what Workload Map calls an instance. podTemplateSpecPath points to each Job’s pod template. scaleDefinition uses jq : the number of pods per replicated Job equals replicas times parallelism , which is why the example manifest sets parallelism explicitly. instanceIdPath takes each instance’s name from .spec.replicatedJobs[].name , which is how “leader” and “worker” show up as distinct roles instead of three anonymous Jobs.
